battleship-potemkin-1925.gazette: The mutiny is real: June 1905, the crew of the Potemkin refusing maggoty meat off Odessa, officers thrown overboard. Odessa saw killing that week; the staircase did not. The Primorsky Stairs have been known as the Potemkin Steps ever since — a landmark named for something that happened only on film.

on-the-waterfront-1954.gazette: Budd Schulberg built the script out of Malcolm Johnson's New York Sun series on racketeering along the New York docks, reporting that took the Pulitzer in 1949. Kazan shot on the Hoboken piers through the winter, with working longshoremen filling the crowds. The shape-up staged in the film was a hiring system, not a plot device.

death-by-hanging-1968.gazette: Ri Chin'u, a Zainichi Korean teenager in Tokyo, was convicted in the 1958 Komatsugawa Incident of killing two schoolgirls and hanged in 1962, at twenty-two. Ōshima opens not on drama but on procedure — the chamber, the trapdoor, the officials and their assigned roles, itemized the way the state itemizes them. Japan hangs its condemned by that same method today.
death-by-hanging-1968.prism: Getting the procedure exactly right is the whole maneuver: once the gallows works precisely as the manual says, whatever goes wrong afterward can't be filed under sloppiness. The state is left no room to call it an aberration.

boy-1969.gazette: In 1966 the Japanese papers carried a family that had made a business of the roads — the father handling the settlement talk, the mother the tears, the child stepping into traffic. Ōshima followed the route rather than the courtroom, shooting town by town across the country and north toward Hokkaido. The boy's job was to be hit and not be badly hurt.

the-enigma-of-kaspar-hauser-1974.gazette: Kaspar Hauser walked into Nuremberg in May 1828 carrying a letter and barely able to speak, and was dead of a stab wound five years later in Ansbach. Herzog kept the documented outline and cast Bruno S., a street musician who had spent much of his life in institutions, to stand inside it. The film ends where the record ends: on the autopsy table, with a clerk delighted to have found an explanation.

in-the-realm-of-the-senses-1976.gazette: Sada Abe strangled Kichizō Ishida in a Tokyo inn in May 1936 and was arrested days later still carrying what she had cut from him; the interrogation transcripts survive and are startling in their candor. Ōshima made the picture as a Japanese-French co-production and shipped the negative to Paris, since the footage could not legally be developed at home. He was later prosecuted in Tokyo over the published stills, and acquitted.
in-the-realm-of-the-senses-1976.prism: The 1936 police file is more explicit than the film was ever permitted to be — the state wrote the record down, then went to court over the picture of it. Abe served five years and walked out; the case against Ōshima's book was still running long after the uncut film had played everywhere outside Japan.

fast-times-at-ridgemont-high-1982.gazette: Cameron Crowe was twenty-two and already on staff at Rolling Stone when he enrolled at a San Diego high school as a senior and stayed the year. The 1981 book kept the pseudonyms and the specifics: the mall jobs, the wages, the abortion, the arithmetic of passing. Heckerling left most of it in.

veronika-voss-1982.gazette: Sybille Schmitz was a UFA star in the 1930s and effectively unemployable in the Federal Republic by the 1950s; she died of an overdose in 1955, under the care of a physician who kept her supplied with morphine. Fassbinder shot the story in blown-out black and white, the glamour lighting of the period's own films turned punishing. He took the Golden Bear in February 1982 and was dead by June.

rain-man-1988.gazette: Barry Morrow met Kim Peek in Texas in 1984 — a man who read two pages at once, one with each eye, and carried thousands of books in memory — and the character came out of that meeting. Hoffman spent months with Peek and other diagnosed savants before shooting; the mannerisms were borrowed rather than devised. Peek was not autistic. He was born without a corpus callosum.
rain-man-1988.prism: The film taught a generation what autism looks like, and what it showed them was modeled on a man who didn't have it. Savant abilities are rare among autistic people; after 1988 they became the first thing strangers expected to find.

the-thin-blue-line-1988.gazette: Errol Morris went to Dallas to interview the psychiatrist whose courtroom testimony had sent men to death row and came away with Randall Dale Adams, convicted in 1976 of shooting a police officer at a traffic stop. The film restaged that shooting several ways, each version matching a different witness's account, and ended on a tape recorder holding David Harris's confession. Adams walked out of prison in 1989, less than a year after the film opened.

i-love-you-to-death-1990.gazette: In Allentown, Pennsylvania, in 1983, Frances Toto and a set of hired accomplices spent weeks trying to kill her husband Anthony — spiked food first, then two bullets fired into his head at close range. He survived, forgave her, and stayed married. Kasdan filmed it as a comedy, which is more or less how the couple told it afterward.

amistad-1997.gazette: The captives aboard La Amistad rose off the Cuban coast in the summer of 1839 and were seized weeks later by a U.S. revenue cutter near Long Island, which turned a shipboard revolt into a property dispute in the federal courts. John Quincy Adams, then seventy-three and sitting in the House, argued the case before the Supreme Court in 1841 and won. The survivors reached Sierra Leone the following year.
amistad-1997.prism: The Court did not rule that slavery was wrong. It ruled that these particular men had been taken in violation of a treaty Spain itself had signed, which made them nobody's property — a win narrow enough to send thirty-odd people home and leave everyone born into slavery in the United States exactly where they stood.

almost-famous-2000.gazette: Lester Bangs appears under his own name, and the advice he hands over — be honest and unmerciful — is advice he actually handed over. Crowe was fifteen when Rolling Stone put him on the road with touring bands, young enough that his age was a thing to be managed. Bangs had been dead eighteen years by the time an actor said his lines back to him.

erin-brockovich-2000.gazette: PG&E's compressor station at Hinkley used hexavalent chromium as a rust inhibitor in its cooling towers and released the wastewater into unlined ponds, from which it reached the town's groundwater. The 1996 settlement ran to $333 million, split among more than six hundred residents — at the time the largest ever paid in a U.S. direct-action suit. Hinkley has been emptying out ever since, PG&E buying the place back parcel by parcel.

the-gleaners-and-i-2000.gazette: Varda shot it herself on the small digital cameras that had just become cheap enough to carry alone, trailing people who take what a harvest leaves behind and what a market throws out. A lawyer in judicial robes stands in a cabbage field and reads aloud the provision that has made gleaning lawful in France since a royal edict of 1554. Between the field and the bins she films Millet's canvas, then her own hands.
the-gleaners-and-i-2000.prism: The right is centuries old and the work is drudgery, and the film keeps both facts in the frame at once — the law permits gleaning, it doesn't confer any dignity on the gleaner. Varda counts herself in: she's picking up images nobody would have funded, on a camera finally cheap enough to make that possible.
